Tech Report: Coffee could have anti-aging benefits. Here’s why.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are a handful of foods and beverages—red wine, eggs, and cooking oils—whose reputations tend to pendulum-swing routinely between “lifesaving” and “death sentence.” I usually hedge my bets by eating these confusing foods in moderation.
  • The one item I have trouble consuming in moderation might be the most contentious of all: coffee.
  • Despite my unwavering devotion to coffee, the jury is still out on whether my daily fix is actually good for my health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are a handful of foods and beverages—red wine, eggs, and cooking oils—whose reputations tend to pendulum-swing routinely between “lifesaving” and “death sentence.” I usually hedge my bets by eating these confusing foods in moderation.

The one item I have trouble consuming in moderation might be the most contentious of all: coffee. I am so hopelessly addicted to the stuff that I usually need at least one cup of coffee before going out to meet a friend for coffee.

Despite my unwavering devotion to coffee, the jury is still out on whether my daily fix is actually good for my health. Throughout my lifetime, coffee has variously been purported to protect my heart, disrupt its rhythm, reduce my risk of cancer, and increase it. All I know is it helps me become a fully conscious person every morning. But could my coffee habit actually reduce wrinkles and help me age more gracefully?

A new study conducted at Texas A&M suggests that certain compounds in coffee might protect the body against aging and inflammation.

According to recent reports, however, according to Dr. Dung Trinh, the chief medical officer at Healthy Brain Clinic in Long Beach, California, it’s probably too soon to pop open the champagne (or brew a celebratory pot) over the potential perks of your coffee habit.

“It’s far too early to treat coffee—or caffeic acid—as an anti-aging intervention,” Trinh tells Popular Science.

According to recent reports, despite its inconsistent status as a health food, coffee has been consistently linked to longer life and a lower likelihood of certain diseases, though it’s not certain why. The Texas A&M study, led by Dr. Stephen Safe, focused on a cellular receptor called NR4A1.

It has been revealed that NR4A1 is a protein that regulates how cells respond to stress and damage. The study found that several compounds in coffee, particularly polyphenols—plant compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties—bind to the NR4A1 receptor. One of these polyphenols, caffeic acid, is found in coffee and many other plants and, despite its name, has nothing to do with caffeine. These compounds seem to promote NR4A1’s protective effects, including mitigating cellular damage and slowing the growth of cancer cell line in laboratory models.

In other words, the harder your NR4A1 proteins are working, the better your cells may be at fending off damage. Sign me up!

According to recent reports, after researchers removed NR4A1 from cells in the lab, those benefits stopped, suggesting this receptor may help produce them. So, if coffee really helps NR4A1 do its job, we might just have a new anti-aging drink on our hands.

Interestingly, caffeine does not appear to play a key part in this mechanism, Trinh says. Instead, those benefits seem to come from coffee’s other compounds, like caffeic acid and its fellow polyphenols.

It has been revealed that “What stood out to me was that the story was not really about caffeine,” he claims. “I also found it interesting that the researchers did more than simply show that these compounds could bind to the receptor—they demonstrated NR4A1-dependent effects in cells. That makes the mechanism more compelling.”.

Translation: The study didn’t just show that coffee compounds attach to NR4A1; it revealed that this binding actually seems to activate the protein’s protective effects.

Consistent with this, the study also found that decaf coffee demonstrated similar protective effects on the lab cells, providing further evidence that coffee’s benefits may not have anything to do with caffeine at all.

“One of the interesting messages from this paper is that coffee should not be thought of as simply a delivery system for caffeine,” Trinh says. “Caffeic acid, chlorogenic acid, ferulic acid, and several other coffee compounds all interacted with NR4A1, while caffeine showed much more variable NR4A1-related activity.”.

So, coffee’s superpower might not come from caffeine at all, at least when it comes to anti-aging benefits.

Before you start guzzling triple lattes in the name of cellular protection, know that “more” does not always mean “better.”.

Recent findings suggest that “We simply cannot infer from this study that more coffee means more NR4A1 benefit,” Trinh indicates. This is because the researchers studied coffee extracts and purified compounds in a lab setting rather than giving human subjects increasing amounts of coffee and measuring NR4A1 activity. Plus, in human biology, it’s possible to have too much of a good thing, Trinh says.

“At some point, additional coffee can bring unwanted effects from caffeine, including sleep disruption, anxiety, palpitations, or increases in blood pressure in susceptible people,” he states. “Those effects could counteract other health benefits. So, this study should not be interpreted as establishing either an optimal number of cups or a dose-response relationship for this pathway.”.

Trinh adds that as compelling as the study’s findings are, he doesn’t yet believe they justify changing recommendations around coffee consumption.

Earlier studies have linked coffee drinking to living longer and to better outcomes for some age-related conditions, Trinh says. But those studies couldn’t explain why. This one offers “one possible biological explanation,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that like most early-stage research, Trinh states, this study can’t be applied to humans sipping their morning “cup of ambition.” Much of the work used a specific cancer cell in the lab, along with mouse immune cells, rather than testing regular human coffee drinkers directly. And while the study identified a potentially promising mechanism, it’s not clear how this mechanism will translate to human health outcomes.

Ultimately, Trinh indicates, no single food or compound is likely to be the deciding factor in how well we age.

Sources indicate that for a coffee addict like myself, though, these findings are the best kind of wake-up call. Coffee may or may not turn back the clock, but it does stop me from hitting snooze 15 times.

“The much bigger determinants of healthy aging remain things such as regular physical activity, good sleep, avoiding smoking, controlling blood pressure and metabolic risk, maintaining social and cognitive engagement, and eating an overall nutritious diet,” Trinh indicates.

“This study is a promising piece of the scientific puzzle, not a prescription for another cup of coffee.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I’ve wanted a leather sofa for many years, but I could never find a color I liked—a detail just as crucial to me as the material. I wasn’t interested in the usual black, brown, or cognac options, instead preferring something less traditional but not squarely trendy. And then I discovered Pottery Barn’s Jake Leather Sofa in Vintage Hunter, which hit my sofa sweet spot, exuding a deep confidence that reads as rich, grounded, and classy. Its sophisticated presence anchors my living room without overpowering the space.

In a recent development, if you don’t love the stately green hue as much as I do, that hardly means the Jake isn’t your room’s match. The sofa’s customization options—another major selling point—are robust: In addition to being able to choose from a broad range of leathers and upholstery colors, I could also select the style of the seat and back cushions, adding up to a piece of furniture that feels more personal than an off-the-sales-floor purchase. With its slim arms, low profile, plush cushions, and bronze-finished metal legs, it strikes a balance between streamlined and inviting.

How much does it cost? Are there payment looks available?

According to recent reports, the cost of the Jake depends on the size, material, and cushion configuration you choose, falling somewhere between $2,000 and $6,000 for most designs. To save yourself from shopping-cart sticker shock, price out the exact model you want, since the leather grade and sofa width can meaningfully change the total. For instance, my 86-inch-wide, 36-inch-deep model in Vintage Hunter retails for $3,999, but a 70-inch-wide, 36-inch-deep loveseat in a Chocolate Performance fabric costs $3,099, and is sometimes on sale for less.

What are the upholstery or customization options? Did you choose any?

Sources indicate that there’s little you can’t choose with the Jake. Available in an extensive selection of leather colors and finishes, you can also pick the number of back cushions you’d like (two or three) and style of seat cushion (two separate or a single bench). For my vintage leather sofa in Hunter, I decided on one bench-style seat cushion and three back cushions.

What is the lead time for customization, manufacturing, and delivery?

It took about six weeks for my sofa to arrive at my home after I ordered it, which felt reasonable for a piece with customized upholstery and cushion selections.

What kind of couch or seating arrangement did you have before, and what drew you to your new couch?

Industry observers note that my previous sofa was a smaller turquoise felt sleeper from Mopio that I bought on Amazon; its blue undertones made it feel brighter and more casual. I loved the feel, but dog hair got caught in it easily and was hard to vacuum. This Hunter shade is deeper, moodier, and much closer to the sophisticated design I had envisioned for the room.

What was the delivery process like? What was the assembly process like? How long did it take, and how many people did it require?

Industry observers note that receiving the sofa could not have been easier, thanks to Pottery Barn’s included white-glove delivery service. Two people brought the sofa into my home, placed it where I wanted it, and assembled it on the spot. The entire process took about 10 minutes. For a substantial piece of furniture like this sofa, the luxury delivery experience was a major advantage.

Industry observers note that what are the dimensions? How does it fit in your space? Would it be better suited for a certain type of home?

Industry observers note that I chose the 85-inch-wide version, which measures 36 inches deep and 32 inches high, and it fits my apartment almost perfectly. It feels generous enough to function as the room’s main seating option without commandeering the full focus of the room. I would recommend this size for a midsize living area, provided that the access points can accommodate its width. As always, measuring the doorway, elevator, stairwell, and turning radius before you click “buy” is just as crucial as measuring the piece’s final spot.

Sit test: Is it comfortable? Does it feel well-made? Does the couch have a tendency to sag?

Comfort is where the Jake has exceeded my expectations. It feels supportive and substantial, and the cushions have held their shape without developing an obvious sag. In the four to five months I’ve had the Jake, several visitors have already stayed over and shared that they’ve experienced restful nights on this couch.

Sources indicate that the only recurring quirk I’ve experienced is that the seat cushion occasionally slides forward a smidge. It is easy to nudge back into place and has never become a serious annoyance. It’s also entirely possible that this funky detail has more to do with my sitting tendencies than the sofa’s construction.

Is the sofa suitable for particular decor styles and if so, which?

Sources indicate that the Jake naturally fits with modern and contemporary interiors. Its low, linear profile, narrow arms, and metal legs provide a clean architectural quality, while the Hunter leather adds depth and character. However, with the right design elements in place, the sofa would also look at home in decidedly relaxed spaces, with warm woods, woven textiles, vintage pieces, or more traditional accessories.

Is it durable and practical in a modern home?

According to recent reports, despite its sophisticated appearance, this sofa isn’t your grandfather’s precious showpiece that exists for looking at and not sitting on. Rather, I’ve found it to be durable, practical, and comfortable to actually use daily.

Recent findings suggest that but that’s just for humans; pets are the bigger consideration here. I have a dog, and a few scratches have already appeared on the leather. My current remediation system is to cover the sofa with a sheet when we are home and remove it before guests arrive. It works, but anyone hoping for completely carefree pet ownership should be realistic about the care needs of a leather sofa before purchasing this polished piece.

The Jake might fare better with children than with a dog, since typical spills are often easy to address promptly, while claw marks are harder to reverse (if possible to do at all). I am planning to try a leather conditioner to soften the appearance of the scratches, though I have not tested it yet. Before applying any product, I would follow Pottery Barn’s care instructions to spot-test it in an inconspicuous area first. Ultimately, the Jake is probably better suited to a pet-free home, or to any owner willing to go whatever lengths necessary to protect and maintain the leather.

In a recent development, do the photos do this product justice? Was there anything you were surprised to see IRL?

The sofa looks remarkably similar in person to how it appears online, including the depth of the Hunter color and the overall proportions. There was no unpleasant reveal on delivery day; the sofa I had spent weeks picturing was essentially the sofa that arrived.

Recent findings suggest that would the couch be easy to move into another room? Would it be easy to move to another apartment or home by yourself?

While it’s more manageable to move than other full-size leather sofas may be, largely in light of its removable legs and loose cushions, I wouldn’t call the Jake a portable sofa. It’s not modular, but rather comes in a single piece, so moving it to another room or home is certainly not a single-person job. However, assuming the doorways and corners cooperate, rehoming its 85-inch span should be possible, so long as you have help on hand.

Comfort: A+Value: ADelivery and assembly: A+Style: A+Overall couch rating: A.

It has been revealed that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that NATHAN FIELDER HAS become one of the greatest arbiters of what is—or isn’t—the truth. Fielder, whose mainstream career unofficially kicked off with his show Nathan for You, a dry, quasi-documentary, quasi-scripted, quasi-spoof of shows like Undercover Boss, has found a way to level up with each project he’s made over the course of his still relatively short career, each step of the way inviting audiences to not only question the reality of what he’s bringing to the screen, but their own stances and ways of thinking about things broadly.

In a recent development, the road for Fielder has included HBO’s The Rehearsal (another often surreal, often Lynchian project that presents as real, but on a subtextual level asks viewers to question whether any of what he’s depicting was really happening as it was shown) and The Curse, a Showtime/Paramount+ series that he starred in and co-created alongside Emma Stone and Benny Safdie. That show was, surprise, surprise, incredibly thoughtful, layered, and, ultimately, surreal when it comes to its underlying themes of sincerity and intention.

According to recent reports, in a way, all of this has led Fielder to his latest project, the new A24 documentary You Can See Everything. The subject is a fitting one for Fielder: Elizabeth Holmes, the former Theranos CEO and convicted fraudster who was the subject of books (Bad Blood) and television reveals (The Dropout) about her misdeeds. It makes total sense that someone famous for skirting the truth would be of interest for Fielder, a creator who has now spent so much time examining not only the truth, but what audiences might accept as the truth even given some reason not to.

It has been revealed that in 2022, Holmes was sentenced to 11 years and 3 months in federal prison. That’s where You Can See Everything comes in: Holmes and her partner Billy Evans invited Fielder (and a film crew, led by co-director Lance Oppenheim) to join them in a home they were renting for complete access during the 34 days before she reported to federal prison in Bryan, Texas, in May 2023. And the film begins there.

And, quite frankly, if you’re considering seeing You Can See Everything, it’s best to leave it there. Fielder gets the access he was promised in the movie, but the joy of the film isn’t only in this exclusive vision of such a notable figure, but how an artist with such a relationship to the truth engages with someone who so notably has, seemingly, bent it. We also get to see Holmes and Evans shot as human beings, removed from any of the prior media circuses that have surrounded them. Fielder and Oppenheim put a fair camera to everything and let the camera do what was promised: See everything.

Sources indicate that you Can See Everything has been one of the best-reviewed films of the year, and it lives up to the billing. Just when you think you understand what’s happening and what’s going to happen, you’ll be swiftly proven wrong. Just when you think you have a handle on who someone is and what they’re all about… you’ll quickly be proven wrong. The movie is three hours long, which, of course, we know, seems daunting. But by the time it ends, you’ll wish it was going on for three hours more.

Below, we answer some of your questions about You Can See Everything—without spoiling any of the movie’s major twists or turns.

Recent findings suggest that you Can See Everything is now available to watch at home. You can purchase it on Apple TV and rent it on Prime Video—and we suggest doing whichever of those you prefer.

According to recent reports, you Can See Everything is, in essence, two movies in one. The first half of the movie is what the trailer and promotional materials for the movie billed: Nathan Fielder joins Elizabeth Holmes (and her new husband Billy Evans) in a home they rented for the 34 days before she reported to federal prison in 2023. This proves to be just as compelling as you’d imagine, as Holmes and Evans are both completely idiosyncratic characters. Moments like when Fielder indicates Holmes Abbott and Costello’s “Who’s on First” bit are instant classics.

Eventually Holmes reports to prison in Bryan, Texas, and the movie is not even halfway over. It’s at this point that your eyebrow should raise, and you do the ‘leaning forward in seat’ meme—because this is when You Can See Everything gets truly wild. The timeline jumps forward two hours, and Nathan Fielder gets up to some of his mind-bending, Rehearsal-type business. At this point, we see some people’s true colors, and also meet some other unexpected guests and surprises in the movie. This second part of the movie is what will blow your mind, and leave you thinking long after the credits begin to roll.

Sources indicate that you Can See Everything should be an absolute lock for a number of Oscar nominations, including Best Picture. And it should be a strong contender in one of the acting categories for one person whose appearance we will not be spoiling in this story.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim are the co-directors of You Can See Everything, and both have been key figures in American film and television culture for the last decade.

According to recent reports, fielder is a Canadian-born actor and director (and childhood friend of Seth Rogen) who rose to fame as the creator and star of Comedy Central’s Nathan for You. He’s dabbled in acting here and there—including a role as a limo driver in Rogen’s underrated holiday comedy The Night Before and in the sensational limited series The Curse—but his real calling has come in mind-bending documentary/comedy series like The Rehearsal. In season 2 of The Rehearsal, for example, Fielder actually got his pilot’s license while exploring the aviation industry. (And that was filmed between part 1 and part 2 of You Can See Everything, which is just bananas.).

Oppenheim, who is only 30, has also established himself as one of the best documentarians in the business. His movies Some Kind of Heaven and Spermworld along with his HBO series Ren Faire are deeply layered portrayals of very real people in very real situations; he shoots these documentaries in styles completely different from anyone else, though, lighting them like cinematic spectacles rather than what you probably think of as a documentary in your mind. (Some of the cinematography in You Can See Everything is unbelievably beautiful.).

Primetime, A24’s film about Chris Hansen and To Catch a Predator that came out last month and starred Robert Pattinson, Skyler Gisondo, and Merritt Wever, was Oppenheim’s scripted feature debut.

It has been revealed that it probably helps to have information on Elizabeth Holmes’s case—which we recommend getting from any number of sources: The Dropout was the name of the Hulu series that starred Amanda Seyfried as Holmes, but it was also a well-researched and reported podcast that served as the show’s basis. There’s also an HBO documentary called The Inventor and a book called Bad Blood. Any of this would make for a good source for the crimes Holmes was accused of committing. The movie also includes a very brief recap of her case in the early going—not exhaustive, but enough to get the idea.

In a recent development, it does also make sense to have an idea of who Fielder is, what he does, and how he engages with his subjects. We recommend HBO’s The Rehearsal for that, but it’s not 100 percent necessary to enjoy and appreciate the film.

That’s the question, isn’t it? You Can See Everything explores the idea of truth, lies, perspective, and even documentary filmmaking itself. If it makes the most sense to you to take all of You Can See Everything at face value, then please go for it. If you feel the need to question everything, well, that’s okay too. That’s what makes Fielder’s work so unique and so immersive—you can think about it about 100 different ways, and no understanding or interpretation is wrong. It’s set up to feel like a kaleidoscope. You can understand something one way, but maybe something pops up, and suddenly you can’t think about it that way anymore. That’s the point—and that’s what you’ll think about long after the credits roll.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

It has been revealed that the largest national forest in the United States, Tongass covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in the region. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

Recent findings suggest that according to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

Breaking: Iceland’s first wind farm comes with a water-saving bonus

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.
  • Vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads.
  • Landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power manufacturer, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.

Vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads. And Iceland’s windiest months coincide with the time of year when less water flows into its reservoirs.

Landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power manufacturer, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026. The first 14 turbines are online; another 14 will be installed in a second phase, and the entire wind farm is expected to be operating by the end of 2027.

It has been revealed that once complete, Vaðölduver will have 120 megawatts (MW) of capacity. When I met with the folks at Landsvirkjun in Reykjavik last month, they told me that’s enough to power the equivalent of 90,000 Icelandic households. Vaðalda’s electricity feeds into the grid and is sold through power purchase agreements.

Vaðölduver sits on a lava-and-sand plain east of the Þjórsá River, south of Sultartangi Dam. Landsvirkjun already operates seven hydropower stations in the surrounding Þjórsá and Tungnaá region.

The wind farm was sited in this region of Iceland because the seasons line up nicely.

The winds are strongest in winter, when inflows into hydropower reservoirs can be low. In summer, wind speeds tend to drop, but glacial melt increases water availability for the hydropower system.

Recent findings suggest that when the wind turbines are generating plenty of electricity, Landsvirkjun can ease off hydropower and leave more water in its reservoirs. When the wind drops, hydropower can pick up more of the demand.

That gives the utility more control over when it uses its stored water and helps that water go further.

German wind turbine maker Enercon manufactured Vaðölduver’s turbines. The project also includes a service and maintenance agreement with Enercon.

It has been revealed that landsvirkjun had a decade of experience operating pilot wind turbines before building Vaðölduver. One massive thing they learned: They didn’t need tall towers to find plenty of wind.

In a recent development, there’s little vegetation or other surface obstructions across this unique, exposed landscape. That allows the turbines to capture productive winds closer to the ground than they could at a more wooded or sheltered location.

“Lower” is relative, of course. The turbines still reach 150 meters (492 feet) at their highest blade tip.

The wind farm covers 17.1 square kilometers (6.6 square miles). Twenty-five turbines are rated at 4.26 MW each, and the remaining three at 4.5 MW. Landsvirkjun’s presentation puts annual generation at 440 GWh and lists a P50 net efficiency figure of 43%, which is considered strong for onshore wind.

It has been revealed that the ability to tap into existing infrastructure was a major factor in Landsvirkjun’s site selection. Where a wind farm goes affects its cost, its environmental footprint, and the people who live nearby.

Landsvirkjun also identifies active engagement with communities and other stakeholders as essential to building wind projects. At Vaðölduver, the immediate task is to finish the remaining 14 turbines while the first phase completes its trial runs.

It has been revealed that the company sees wind as a potential third pillar of Iceland’s electricity supply alongside hydropower and geothermal. Vaðölduver shows how those resources can work together, with wind adding generation while helping conserve stored water.

Iceland is a world leader in clean energy. It generates nearly 100% of its electricity from renewable sources, combining hydropower fueled by glacial runoff and rivers (around 70%) and geothermal energy (around 30%).

Over 90% of Icelandic households use direct geothermal hot water for space heating and hot water, while the remaining homes use renewable electricity.

Industry observers note that but it’s got the same grid capacity challenges as every other country. Adding wind – and anything else that uses power – means paying close attention to what the grid can handle. Iceland has an isolated transmission system, so maintaining stability and ensuring sufficient capacity are increasingly important as the country develops more projects.

While in Reykjavik, I met with the Minister of the Environment, Energy and Climate, Jóhann Páll Jóhannsson, who told me that the Icelandic grid’s capacity is expected to grow from 20 TWh to 24-25 TWh within a decade. Jóhannsson also said that he is pro-data center and that investors are keen to establish more of them in the country.

It has been revealed that when I asked Jóhannsson and his team, as well as the teams at Landsvirkjun and publicly owned ON Power, Iceland’s second-largest electricity generator and largest EV charger network, about grid expansion plans to handle that pipeline, they all remarked that legislative reforms were being passed to speed up energy permitting processes. There is also financing in place to grow the grid. The physical transmission network is being expanded, but the process is slow because NIMBYism is creating bottlenecks.

In learning about latest and completed Icelandic power projects during my visit, it was apparent that the companies in the power and geothermal heat sector regularly collaborate on projects – everyone brings their expertise to the table and works for the common good (yes, really).

But what was striking in discussions about grid expansion was that there seemed to be no plans to pitch in with the Icelandic transmission system operator (TSO), Landsnet hf. It seemed that the plan was to let the TSO come up with the solutions on its own. At most, Jóhannsson’s team noted its legislative reform “opened the door” to possible grid innovations.

When I asked the Landsvirkjun team whether they were considering working with the TSO on distributed energy resource (DER) projects like virtual power plants and onsite battery storage for its heavy-industry clients, which make up 80% of its business, they said they hadn’t considered it.

I often wonder why Quebec hasn't followed this strategy. They have huge dams with world-leading power connections, and one of the concern they are facing is a lack of water to refill those dams, due to several years of relative drought. I know it costs a lot to build wind power up north, but siting a project there would re-use their massive investment in power lines. The dams would act as gigantic batteries, because they wouldn't need to drain their reservoirs when the wind is blowing.

Recent findings suggest that iceland has earned its reputation as a clean energy leader. Bringing that same collaborative and creative approach to expanding its grid would help it keep setting an example for the rest of the world.

WHEN YOUR HOME gym is short on square footage like mine, you need to carefully think about every piece of equipment before it earns its rightful spot. That’s exactly why kettlebells are a staple in my setup. Over time, I’ve built a small but mighty collection—and every single one gets regular use.

Sources indicate that A huge perk of kettlebells is that they don’t hog a lot of space (even in a compact home gym) and are relatively inexpensive, indicates Tyneka Pack, CPT. These are versatile strength-training tools, too, allowing you to get in a full-body workout, along with explosive power movements, says kettlebell specialist Taylor Beebe, CPT.

Recent findings suggest that as with any fitness equipment, improper use of kettlebells can lead to injury. That’s why most trainers, including Beebe, recommend getting coaching on how to use kettlebells before diving in (peep our how to get started with kettlebell exercises guide).

Like dumbbells, kettlebells come in a wide range of weights, materials, and grips, so it’s important to determine which type you’re in the market for before you buy.

After testing a handful of kettlebells, this cast-iron option from Amazon Basics earns its spot at the top of our list because of its budget price tag and versatile weight options. The weight range from 10 to 60 pounds has allowed me to ramp up my training intensity over time.

This kettlebell has consistently been my go-to and favorite even as I’ve expanded my collection. They’re surprisingly sturdy and durable, even after two years of use. WH fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief also loves this model and has multiple in her home gym, too.

Recent findings suggest that I own it in several weight sizes, and it has a compact shape that’s great for every kettlebell exercise imaginable. The grip is slightly textured and wide enough to do one- or two-handed exercises, but petite enough for smaller hands like mine. I can confidently hold it, even during potential wall-breaking moves like swings, and it’s comfortable to hold, whether I’m doing one set or five.

While these weights have a lot going for them, there is one con: There is no vinyl coating on the bottom (although there is a vinyl version, which WH editors also love). To avoid scratching my floors, I have to set it down carefully or use a mat underneath.

Sources indicate that many people prefer a competition-style kettlebell due to its uniform design that’s ideal for high reps and technical moves. The Rep Fitness Adjustable Kettlebell offers a competition-style kettlebell shape with adjustable weights, giving you plenty of space-saving mileage out of one tool.

In a recent development, this kettlebell is well-designed, stacking five weights in one relatively compact design. (Weight ranges include 8 to 16 kilograms, 16 to 24 kilograms, and 20 to 40 pounds.) To adjust the weight, just push down on the dial with two fingers, twist to your desired weight, and lift. It has a rubber base to protect your floors although—heads up—the rubber coating is only there when you use the kettlebell’s full weight. Otherwise, you’ll want to set down your kettlebell gingerly.

Sources indicate that REP’s adjustable kettlebell is made from cast iron and feels durable. The textured handle is easy to grip and has plenty of space for two-handed moves, although it feels slightly wider than others. If space is a premium at your place and you’re looking to grow with your kettlebell, this is a solid choice.

Read More: Best Compact Home Gym Equipment.

In a recent development, if you prefer a more traditional competition-style kettlebell, keep scrolling. But if you’re on the hunt for a highly versatile weight that aims to combine the attributes of a kettlebell with those of a dumbbell and a dual-grip medicine ball, the YBell Neo Series is worth consideration.

This weight is perfect for my needs—it’s relatively compact and offers multiple ways to grip, thanks to its unique pyramid-style design. I can use it for everything from biceps curls to lunges, though it’s not ideal for swings.

The grip on this is perfection. It features a neoprene outer layer to create a slightly sticky feel with impressive gripping power, so I’m not stressed about accidentally flinging it across the room during swings. The wide handle leaves enough room for one- or two-handed exercises, but it may feel a little crowded using both mitts at once if your hands are on the larger side.

Sources indicate that you have three different spots you can grip on the outside of this weight, along with an inside bar that’s ideal for dumbbell-style work. While the sides are rounded, I found it was relatively easy to rest the YBell on its base or sides to save space.

Recent findings suggest that the only potential downside of this weight is that it tops out at 26 pounds. If you’re interested in doing heavier lifting, you’ll need to upgrade to a different device.

Sources indicate that A coated kettlebell like this one from Yes4All protects your floors in case of butterfingers through a thoughtfully wrapped coating up the bottom third of the handle. The handle itself makes for a comfortable grip. Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi says, “I have the 15-pound model and I never feel it slipping away from me when squatting or doing Russian twists.” It comes in five-pound increments up to 65 pounds, giving you plenty of options.

Industry observers note that while I wouldn’t recommend tossing this on your floor at home, the kettlebell doesn’t make a loud noise when it’s dropped, unlike uncoated models. It’s also worth pointing out it’s very affordable, similar to our best overall.Just note the bottom of the kettlebell is not entirely flat, which can be tricky if you’re trying exercises like uneven pushups (with one hand placed through the handles of a KB).

Sand kettlebells are a highly portable option that allows you to add a little more instability to your kettlebell workouts. The GoRuck Sand Kettlebell is built tough thanks to its Cordura nylon design and multiple closure system, so you don’t have to stress about accidentally spilling its contents all over the place.

GoRuck’s kettlebell has a teardrop-style shape that works well for many exercises. This kettlebell arrives empty, so you’ll fill it up with sand prior to use. Pro tip: use playground sand available at home improvement stores for this. The reinforcing on nearly all of the seams and bottoms means you can toss this on the ground without worrying about it flying open and spilling sand everywhere.

This style of kettlebell isn’t for everyone, but if you’re looking to add the extra challenge of sandbag training to your kettlebell workouts, this sand kettlebell design will take a lot of abuse and holds up well over time.

In a recent development, “When choosing the correct weight for your kettlebell, it is notable to consider your exercise,” claims Almoni Ellis, CSCS, CPT. She says that people generally are able to use heavier weights when doing purely lower-body exercises, but that those weights may be too heavy for a person when they’re doing a move like an overhead press, for example.

Sources indicate that that said, there’s no one-size-fits-all starting point. Your experience level and current strength come into play, so if you’re unsure where to begin, try testing different weights at a local gym or consider ordering two sizes to see what feels best. As your strength improves, you can gradually increase the weight, adds Pack.

Sources indicate that the most common option for general strength training is the cast-iron kettlebell, which works well for everything from goblet squats to cleans to swings. These are the kettlebells you’ll most often see in home gyms and fitness classes.

It has been revealed that ellis and Pack recommend choosing a cast iron or steel kettlebell because they’re the most durable and long-lasting materials. “Kettlebells [that are] made up of plastic[...] don’t last as long,” Pack claims.

However, most adjustable kettlebells are made with some plastic components, which is necessary for the design. As for vinyl-coated kettlebells, they’re usually made of cast iron with a vinyl coating to prevent damage to floors.

Recent findings suggest that handle thickness plays a role in both comfort and performance. “Thicker handles can help build grip strength, but they may be more challenging for beginners to control,” claims Pack.

The handle’s coating and texture matter just as much. A slightly textured surface can help you maintain a secure grip, especially during dynamic or high-rep movements. Slick handles, on the other hand, can become slippery as your hands sweat—raising the risk of losing your grip, Pack adds. If you’re training with kettlebell that has a slick grip, consider using workout chalk or liquid chalk during moves like swings.

To choose the best kettlebells, I consulted three personal trainers who regularly work with kettlebells: Taylor Beebe, CPT, Tyneka Pack, CPT, and Almoni Ellis, CSCS. I also got feedback from Women’s Health fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief, NASM-CPT, who is a certified trainer.

Recent findings suggest that based on their feedback, I focused on crucial features to look for in these super versatile strength-training tools. I then tested some of the most popular kettlebells out there. Each was put through a slew of workouts to test its efficiency, durability, weight, material, and grip. Because every person’s budget is different, I made sure to include kettlebells with a range of price points.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that “It was like Frankenstein,” states the husband of the shingled postmodern house on Rhode Island’s rocky coast that he shares with his wife and their three young-adult children. Built by his father in the 1980s, the house occupies an extraordinary site overlooking the Atlantic ocean and an expansive marsh. But successive additions had left it architecturally disjointed. The Manhattan-based couple, fresh from updating a Litchfield County weekend retreat with AD PRO Directory designer James “Ford” Huniford, asked him to take another look. “We were thrilled to have him try to rethink this house for us,” says the wife, “which may have been easier in retrospect to just knock down.”.

Industry observers note that in a favorite sitting room, which Huniford reconfigured from a triangle into a rectangle, rattan Audoux-Minet armchairs and a custom sofa flanked by 1930s Kittinger pedestal tables wear cushions covered in a Colefax and Fowler chintz. The walls, clad in Scalamandré wallpaper, display 1950s ceramic plates from Italy’s Amalfi Coast, while an antique French chandelier hangs overhead. The coffee table is custom and the carpet is from Sacco. “I was impressed with [Ford’s] ability to take risks and do things that were different than he had done,” notes the wife, pointing to the chintz fabric, “and we were very happy with the outcome.”.

Industry observers note that the French wicker barrel chair with a Jasper-covered cushion and a custom sofa, upholstered in Pierre Frey, complete the seating arrangement around a vintage coffee table. Layered beneath are rugs from Doris Leslie Blau and Sacco, the former a midcentury Scandinavian design. Rococo side tables each support a 1930s Camille Tharaud vase lamp, while the 1961 patinated-brass ceiling lights by Jacques Quinet are from Galerie Apaganthe.

Rather than impose a conventional beach-house aesthetic, Huniford sought to evoke the early-20th-century summer houses of Latest England while preserving the existing structure’s character. His references ranged from the work of architect Fred Lincoln Savage on Maine’s Mount Desert Island to Kilkare, a Victorian oceanfront estate in Wainscott, New York. New rooflines, structural bump-outs, covered porches, traditional divided-light windows, and detailing brought a sense of accumulated history, even as the house was winterized and its systems updated. Expanded interiors and improved flow were achieved with remarkably little change to the overall footprint. “To me,” claims Huniford, “the luxury is in the detail of the craft.”.

Garden-inspired Ferrick Mason wallpaper enlivens the jewel-box powder room, where a vintage pedestal sink is paired with a Samuel Heath faucet. Antique Italian sconces flank a vintage Italian mirror from Donzella, while a green 1970s pendant by Hans-Agne Jakobsson for Staff and a Rug & Kilim rug complete the space.

Sources indicate that in the dining area, English whitewashed painted chairs upholstered in a Pierre Frey fabric surround a custom table draped with an antique coarse-linen buggy blanket and topped with Vallauris woven plates and a 1960s Émile Tessier cachepot. Above hangs a 19th-century Dutch brass chandelier from Brownrigg, while Josef Albers color case studies enliven the walls. “What I love about Ford is: I was like, ‘Are you sure that we should paint the walls yellow?’” the wife recalls of Huniford’s custom paint selection. “And he’s like, ‘I don’t know. This is a whole latest world for me, but yeah, I think we should.’”.

Industry observers note that inside, the designer took his cues from the wraparound vistas and shifting natural light, particularly during the summer months, when the family spends most of its time here. “The ocean can be dark black and then it can be blue and then it can be green,” says Huniford. “I love the sea. It’s such a magical thing.” That ever-changing palette informed rooms of relaxed refinement, where the mix includes English, French, and early American furnishings, many slipcovered in upholstery washed to achieve an effortlessly lived-in quality. “They don’t like clutter, and they don’t like fussiness,” Huniford notes of his clients. “They like function, and they love form.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the kitchen, striped wall covering by Maresca Textiles provides a lively backdrop for vintage opaline globe wall lights, Newport Brass plumbing fixtures, and a collection of vintage ceramics and tableware. A French bobbin chair is from Andrew Spindler Antiques & Design.

According to recent reports, in a newly added pantry adjoining the dining area, new and vintage tabletop treasures include Tiffany & Co. salt and pepper mills, a stoneware pitcher by Bennington Potters, green Dieulefit glasses, and bowls from Paula Rubenstein.

In a recent development, the palette of another sitting room takes its cues from the nearby ocean. Braided-rattan lounge chairs by Henry Link, sourced at Brimfield and topped with cushions in a Décors Barbares fabric, flank an armless sofa with Christopher Farr–covered seat cushions and back cushions upholstered in a Fabricut textile. The coffee table, side table, and lamp are vintage; the ceiling fixture is by Schoolhouse, and the carpet is from Stark.

Yet there is plenty of playfulness beneath the restraint. Huniford introduced an unexpected palette and, in a first for both designer and clients, chintz. In the open-plan living, kitchen, and dining areas, where windows were left free of treatments, sea-glass-green doors complement wide-plank walls painted a buttery yellow. Colorful works by Josef Albers, a favorite of the husband and sourced by Huniford, provide a graphic counterpoint near a dining table surrounded by whitewashed chairs and draped with an antique rough-linen buggy cover. In an adjacent sitting room, rattan furniture brightened by cushions in a radiant Colefax & Fowler floral take center stage. “I never thought in a million years that I’d have chintz in my house,” admits the wife, “but it now happens to be my favorite fabric.”.

A dreamy layering of florals defines the primary bedroom, from Temple Studio wallpaper and a headboard and bed skirt in Bennison Fabrics textiles to a Matouk bedspread and pillowcases and a blanket from The Company Store. A vase and lamp from Huniford’s vintage stock sit atop a side table from Fernyhough Antiques.

An English neoclassical mahogany desk by Kittinger, sourced on Chairish, is where the husband prefers to work while taking in ocean views. The desk chair and lamp are vintage, while a dhurrie rug from Rug & Kilim anchors the space. The window treatments are fashioned from a Savel textile.

In the primary bath, vintage painted sconces with glass shades illuminate a custom mirror and Grand Brass plumbing fixtures. A series of framed vintage French dried botanical specimens hangs above a vintage blue firkin.

Alan Campbell wallpaper sets the tone in this bedroom, where a vintage bed and console—the latter painted in Benjamin Moore’s Casco Bay—join assorted furnishings from Huniford’s own stock to create a transportive retreat.

It has been revealed that in a guest bedroom, twin beds feature headboards covered in a punchy Designtex print and vintage bedding. A side table sourced on Chairish stands beneath a framed collection of 1920s floral prints.

Sources indicate that for Huniford, whose primary mission is to understand how all of his clients think and live, the goal here was not to reinvent the family’s lifestyle but to make the house better accommodate it. A windowed banquette in a new bump-out beside the dining table has become a favorite gathering spot; its overhead pottery shelf was inspired by a photograph of decorator and fashion editor Chessy Rayner’s Southampton home. The adjacent sitting room, long a center of family life, was transformed from an awkward triangle into a rectangle, allowing the space to function more comfortably. “Our lifestyle in this house,” the husband now says, “did not change.”.

According to recent reports, the three-year undertaking benefited from the couple’s willingness to give Huniford considerable creative freedom, and the time to realize his vision. The result feels as though it has evolved over generations rather than been assembled piecemeal, its newfound polish tempered by a familiar sense of ease. “I think a great house should make you feel welcome and welcoming,” indicates Huniford. And that, it seems, has been the greatest success. As the wife puts it, “Everyone loves to go there.”.

Whenever weather permits, the family gathers for meals on the ocean-facing deck, where vintage Brown Jordan chairs with cushions in a Perennials fabric surround a Laurel Group table dressed with a vintage Italian tablecloth, napkins, and tableware.

Huniford’s design extended beyond the architecture and interiors to the surrounding landscape, where the expansive front lawn gave way to meadow grasses, and an asphalt driveway was replaced with gravel. “I’ve done a few gardens for clients before, and I think [these homeowners] understood my sensibility,” notes Huniford. “They did not want a lot of maintenance or formal gardens.” The staircase leading to the second-floor entrance ranks among the designer’s favorite structural additions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

Recent findings suggest that by 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

According to recent reports, the researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

The researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:.

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:.

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

However, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:.

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she remarked.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

“Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

More than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:.

It has been revealed that “These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” mentioned Kirkpatrick.

She also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Sources indicate that kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick mentioned.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

According to recent reports, “Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an vital factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” mentioned Kirkpatrick.

Hackers use old Bitly links to re-direct to offensive content

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that be wary of the next few shortened website links you click on social media.
  • That’s a polite way of putting it, since many of the hijacked URLs sent unsuspecting people on detours to inappropriate, obscene, and offensive webpages ranging from Wikipedia entries on the Holocaust and 9/11, to vulgar YouTube audio clips.
  • According to recent reports, link-shortening is one of the internet’s simplest and most convenient workarounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that be wary of the next few shortened website links you click on social media. According to the service provider Bitly, its hyperlinks in older tweets from many companies, politicians, and even government accounts are now redirecting to “content unrelated to the original posts.”.

That’s a polite way of putting it, since many of the hijacked URLs sent unsuspecting people on detours to inappropriate, obscene, and offensive webpages ranging from Wikipedia entries on the Holocaust and 9/11, to vulgar YouTube audio clips.

According to recent reports, link-shortening is one of the internet’s simplest and most convenient workarounds. The service typically works by pinning a website’s lengthy, complex URL address to a tidied-up, abbreviated shortcut in a digital registry. This shortened address then redirects anyone who clicks it to their intended online destination.

Well…in theory. Security analysts have tried to warn people about an issue known as “bit rot” for decades. In 2009—about one year after Bitly’s debut—Silicon Valley entrepreneur Joshua Schacter wrote a prescient blog post cautioning against what he felt were potentially serious flaws in the link-shortening “middleman” system. Amid the issues, Schacter cited a “fresh and potentially unreliable” tool that ties an original hyperlink to the “health of a third party.”.

“The shortener may decide a link is a Terms Of Service violation and delete it. If the shortener accidentally erases a database, forgets to renew its domain, or just disappears, the link will break,” he explained. “If a top-level domain changes its policy on commercial use, the link will break. If the shortener gets hacked, every link becomes a potential phishing attack.”.

It has been revealed that it now appears bad actors recently identified countless of these Bitly links previously posted across social media between 2009 and 2014. Although their exact methods aren’t clear, it’s possible they generated their own custom Bitly links using the addresses in the social media posts, then used those to send people to different destinations. Bitly notes its links do not automatically expire, but paid users may redirect existing links.

Sources indicate that many examples were found among the more than 60,000 posts on X from President Donald Trump’s official account. In one of Trump’s previous posts about his golf course in Scotland, the Bitly link temporarily redirected to Wikipedia’s entry on the Epstein Files. Targets also included corporations like McDonald’s, with one of the fast food giant’s 2011 Bitly URLs suddenly linked to Wikipedia’s page about the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.

It has been revealed that not every hijacked post funneled people to upsetting outcomes. Instead of a cybersecurity PSA, the Bitly address in a 2021 post from the FBI briefly linked to a photo of a blubbery seal. Another of Trump’s URLs sent you to the popular video game, Geometry Dash.

In its acknowledgement of the problem on November 15, Bitly reported it had identified and suspended the bad actors’ accounts, and were in the process of “disabling the affected links.”.

“Our Trust and Safety team is working to address the concern and strengthen protections against similar misuse in the future,” Bitly wrote at the time.

As Electrek reported in January, Solarcycle’s Cedartown, Georgia, plant was processing thousands of old solar panels a week when it opened. Solarcycle said the plant could handle up to 5 gigawatts’ worth of panels annually at full capacity, recovering materials such as glass, aluminum, copper, and silver.

Recent findings suggest that the Tennessee plant adds a US refining step. Korea Zinc is developing the facility, called Project Crucible, with US government backing. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that around the world, the number of uncontacted Indigenous tribes continues to dwindle. Indigenous rights advocates estimate that half of the nearly 200 communities still existing in comparative isolation could disappear within a decade, without proper safeguards against climate change, land loss, fame-seeking opportunists, and illegal industrial encroachments. Unfortunately, the situation has apparently grown so dire that some Indigenous groups are reaching out for help—and exposing themselves to potentially deadly foreign diseases in the process.

On November 17, the nonprofit advocacy group Survival International reported a recent incident in which 20 members of the Awá people intentionally contacted local government officials in the Brazilian Amazon. Although proficient hunter-gatherers, the group requested yams before taking them back into the rainforest.

“This is a troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger,” Survival International director Caroline Pearce noted in a statement.

The Awá are one of the world’s last uncontacted Indigenous tribes, whose ties to the Brazilian rainforest stretch back centuries. They faced their first attacks from European settlers during the 1800s, which eventually forced them to adopt a nomadic lifestyle to avoid future encounters. Brazil finally supplied the Awá with settlement areas during the mid-1980s, but it still took years before the government properly invested in demarcated land. In the meantime, numerous deadly interactions with loggers, farmers, and other illegal intruders had reduced the Awá community to barely 300 people. Of those, advocates estimate only about one-third of the hunter-gatherers remain completely isolated from the outside world.

“The Brazilian government must commit the resources necessary to protect [the region of] Arariboia from the loggers and ranchers who are razing it, in flagrant defiance of the law,” Pearce added.

In addition to the advocacy work by Survival International, the Awá are supported by a team of Indigenous members of the Guajajara community known as the Forest Guardians. These volunteers have spent years pushing back against illegal cattle ranchers and loggers attempting to claim land in Arariboia, often dying as a result of their efforts.

“The Forest Guardians have always worked to protect the Awá against encroachment, even at the cost of losing warriors in battle,” the organization remarked. “We demand immediate action from the relevant authorities…to ensure what the Awá believe is best for them, safeguarding their lives, health, safety and dignity. FOR THE AWÁ, FOR THE TENETEHAR [language], AND FOR THE FOREST!”.

Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

📅 01 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1387 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated strategy of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.
  • The reports detail how cardiovascular health challenges can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.
  • The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated strategy of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health challenges can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

It has been revealed that they stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

The authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” said Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”.

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, said the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she said.

“I am incredibly excited to see these fresh reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah noted.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”.

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg said this life-stage breakdown is important, especially for risk reduction.

Industry observers note that she remarked challenges with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg stated.

In a recent development, suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”.

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” said Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive strategy for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”.

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

“These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”.

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are crucial windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” remarked William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”.

The authors note several age-related warning signs of heart concerns. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

Sources indicate that females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” mentioned Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”.

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

The organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

The authors of that report listed several steps they mentioned could reverse these trends. Among them:.

Experts say women can also take action on their own to reduce their risks. Suppogu suggests the following:.

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu remarked.

Industry observers note that weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She mentioned that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

Recent findings suggest that khan stated women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

“Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the crabs are coming.
  • The migration begins with the first rainfall of the wet season, typically in October or November, but can be as late as December or January.
  • According to Christmas Island National Park, the speed and timing of the migration is determined by the moon’s phases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the crabs are coming. Millions upon millions of them. Christmas Island red crabs (Gecarcoidea natalis) have officially begun their annual migration on the tiny Australian territory in the Indian Ocean.

The migration begins with the first rainfall of the wet season, typically in October or November, but can be as late as December or January. Red crabs from all over Christmas Island will leave their homes in the forest at the same time and start their march towards the ocean. Once they reach the ocean, they will mate and spawn. The male crabs lead the migration, while the females join in along the way.

According to Christmas Island National Park, the speed and timing of the migration is determined by the moon’s phases. “Red crabs always spawn before dawn on a receding high-tide during the last quarter of the moon,” the park rangers write. “Incredibly, they know exactly when to leave their burrows to make this lunar date.”.

However, the crabs will wait until the first rainfall to begin their journey, so they sometimes have to hurry. If the rains arrive close to their optimal spawning date, the crabs will move to the ocean very swiftly. If the rain comes early, the crustaceans may take their time, “stopping to eat and drink on their way to the coast.” If rain begins too late to make the spawning date, some of the crabs will remain in their burrows and begin their migration the following month.

Industry observers note that the result is spectacular. Tens of millions of bright red crustaceans the size of a soda can spread out over the 12-mile-wide island on their way to the ocean. They begin their march inland and will reach their destination in about nine days. In 2008, naturalist and documentarian Sir David Attenborough described the annual event as one of his best television moments.

Sources indicate that over the next few days Parks Australia will run livestreams of the migration for about 60 minutes. The exact timing and number of livestreams can’t be scheduled in advance since it is completely dependent on the crabs.

“We will aim to livestream in the morning, but the crabs will have the final say on when and how many days they will venture across the bridge,” the rangers write.

It has been revealed that filming occurs at the red crab bridge, a 16-foot-tall structure built to help the crabs cross the busy road. The crabs will migrate past this bridge for about three to four days.
